newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Danish bank buys into Sweden's banking sector.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Danish bank buys into Sweden's banking sector.

text.p: Denmark's Den Danske Bank made a surprise swoop on Sweden's banking sector on Monday, snapping up the last of the country's provincial banks.
Swedish holding company Lundbergs said it had sold its 76.9 percent stake in Ostgota Enskilda Bank (OEB) to Den Danske Bank at 50.5 crowns a share for a total 2.2 billion crowns ($284 million).
"With Den Danske Bank as a new owner, Ostgota Enskilda Bank will have new possibilites to develop and invest offensively from a very strong base," Lundbergs said in a statement.
"This will be advantageous for OEB's customers as well as their partners and will be favourable for competition as well as the new thinking on the Swedish financial market."
The merger hinged on approval from Sweden's finance inspectorate, Lundbergs said.
The takeover comes as Sweden's banking and finance sector nears the end of a major shakeout.
Last month Swedish banks Swedbank and Foreningsbanken merger to become the country's second largest bank, called ForeningsSparbanken.
Earlier this year Sweden's largest bank Handelsbanken bought mortgage bank Stadshypotek in a 23 billion crown bid.

Analysts said they were surprised by a cross-border move at this late stage in the Sweden's banking sector shake-up because the potential cost savings of the deal were not as obvious as a merger between two Swedish banks.
The move was also unexpected because Swedish financier Fredrik Lundberg, who controls the Lundbergs group, is known in Sweden as a longterm shareholder, analysts said.
Any Nordic merger has been long overshadowed by a much flagged merger between S-E-Banken and state-controlled Nordbanken which analysts said was still to come.
"The last word has not been spoken about S-E-Banken and Nordbanken," said Fiba analyst Jan Dworsky.
"I think a merger between S-E-Banken and Nordbanken will be the last big new structure. It's coming," said another.

Swedish newspaper Dagens Industri quoted unnamed sources on Monday as saying a merger between S-E-Banken and Nordbanken would not take place until after April 29, after S-E-Banken holds its annual shareholders meeting.
The newspaper also said merger speculation fuelled a rise in S-E-Banken's shares on Friday, which ended at a record 84.5 crowns after rising 4.3 percent last week.
OEB's appeal lay in the fact it was the last of Sweden's small to medium sized banking institutions that could be bought, Dworsky said. OEB has 29 branches and about 500 staff.
"It's the only provincial bank left," he said in an interview.
Although the bank is small, it has an advantageous link to Sweden's main nationwide network of automatic teller machines.
"It's a small bank but you have cooperation between it and the larger banks in Sweden," said one Stockholm based analyst.
Analysts seemed to agree that the price was high, and Swedbank analyst Jonny Sylven pointed out that a share redemption programme may have been more favourable to shareholders.
"We did think Ostgota Enskilda should be separate from Lundbergs," said Sylven. "Den Danske buying it was a surprise."
He said the merger process would take a long time and it was difficult to judge how successful it would be.
"It's very difficult for a bank to merge with another bank from a different country," Sylven said.
